purpose: Test plural Latin American and Caribbean structures while preserving Indigenous, Iberian, African-diasporic, national, linguistic, gender, colonial, and diasporic standpoints and their conflicts.

packet_slots.position: conquest-era Indigenous and Iberian encounters over personhood, reason, testimony, natural law, conversion, violence, land, and textual custody
independence and post-independence inquiry on intellectual authenticity, Nuestra América, mestizaje, race, nation, education, and the risks of civilizational synthesis
philosophy and theology of liberation, dependency, exteriority, analectics, praxis, option for the oppressed, and institutional transformation
coloniality of power/knowledge/being, racial classification, modernity, border thinking, pluriversality, and internal decolonial criticism
Latin American, Afro-Latin/Amefrican, Indigenous, and decolonial feminist inquiry on colonial gender, race, body-territory, epistemicide, care, autonomy, and coalition
Francophone, Anglophone, Hispanophone, and diasporic Caribbean inquiry on creolization, relation, opacity, sociogeny, colonial language, plantation worlds, and new humanism

selection_rules: Latin American, Caribbean, Hispanic, Lusophone, Francophone, Indigenous, mestizo, Black, Afro-Latin, and decolonial are different scopes and never synonyms.
Conquest archives preserve asymmetric custody; Indigenous testimony and concepts are not merely data for European debates.
Nation, race, mestizaje, liberation, dependency, coloniality, gender, and creolization remain internally contested rather than regional doctrines.
Spanish, Portuguese, French, English, Creole, and Indigenous-language terms retain their language and translation histories.
No religious, revolutionary, nationalist, racial, gender, land, legal, reparative, or decolonial position becomes Factorium guidance.
